purpose: Vancomycin is a powerful antibiotic used to treat serious bacterial infections, especially those caused by bacteria that are resistant to other antibiotics. It is commonly used for infections like MRSA (a tough staph infection), certain heart infections, bone infections, and a serious gut infection called C. difficile. Doctors often use it when other antibiotics have not worked or are not safe for you.
how_it_works: Vancomycin works by attacking the outer wall that bacteria need to survive. Think of it like pulling bricks out of a wall — without a strong wall, the bacteria fall apart and die. Because it targets bacteria in a unique way, it is effective against bugs that have learned to outsmart other antibiotics.
common_side_effects: The most common side effects include nausea, changes in kidney function, and ringing in the ears. When given through an IV too quickly, it can cause flushing, redness, and itching of the face and neck — this is called Red Man Syndrome and is not a true allergy. You may also experience pain or irritation at the IV site.
warnings: Vancomycin can affect your kidneys and hearing, especially if you take it for a long time or at high doses, so your doctor will check blood levels and kidney function regularly. Tell your doctor if you have kidney problems or hearing loss before starting this medication. Avoid taking it with other medications that can also harm the kidneys. If you develop rash, trouble breathing, or swelling, contact your healthcare provider right away.
typical_dosing: When given by IV for serious infections, the usual adult dose is around 15 to 20 mg per kilogram of body weight every 8 to 12 hours, but your doctor will adjust this based on your weight, kidney function, and blood levels. For C. difficile gut infections taken by mouth, the typical adult dose is 125 mg four times a day for 10 days. Your care team will monitor your blood levels closely to make sure you are getting just the right amount.
